Standard/Heuristic: Nielsen #9: Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors
Location: Appointment Booking page, patient details form
Observation: Submitting the form with one invalid field reloads the page and clears every field, including insurance member ID and date of birth.
Impact: Patients have to re-enter everything after a single typo; some will give up and call instead, or not book at all.
Recommendation: Validate on the client before submit and preserve entered values on server-side errors; move focus to the first invalid field.
At a Glance: One typo on the booking form wipes everything the patient typed, so some patients will abandon the booking.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/book; entered an 8-digit phone number and submitted; all 9 fields cleared on reload

Observation: The booking flow has three steps (location, time, patient details) with no step indicator or count; the URL stays /book throughout.
Impact: Patients can't tell how much is left, and the browser Back button returns them to the homepage, losing their place.
Recommendation: Add a visible step indicator ("Step 2 of 3") and give each step its own history entry so Back works as expected.
At a Glance: Patients booking an appointment can't tell how many steps are left, and pressing Back loses their place.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/book; walked all three steps; Back from step 2 lands on https://example-site.com/

Location: Navigation, page headings, and buttons on all audited pages
Observation: The same action is called "Book an Appointment", "Schedule a Visit", and "Request Care" in different places, and the booking page heading is "New Patient Request".
Impact: Patients aren't sure these lead to the same place, and existing patients may think the booking page isn't for them.
Recommendation: Pick one term ("Book an appointment") and use it in navigation, buttons, and the booking page heading.
At a Glance: The site uses three different names for booking an appointment, so patients can't be sure they're in the right place.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/ (header button, hero CTA), /contact (sidebar), /book (H1)
Instances: 4 pages: Homepage, Appointment Booking, Insurance FAQ, Contact

Observation: No visible focus indicator appears on links, buttons, or fields when navigating by keyboard; suppressed globally in the CSS reset.
Impact: Keyboard-only users cannot tell where they are on the page, making the site difficult or impossible to navigate without a mouse.
Recommendation: Restore visible focus states site-wide as part of the global stylesheet.
At a Glance: Patients who navigate by keyboard can't reliably tell where they are on any page of the site, which is both a real barrier and a compliance risk.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/, /book, /reset-password, /insurance-faq, /contact; global.css rule `*:focus { outline: none }`; tabbed through each page, no focus ring on a, button, input
Instances: 5 pages: Homepage, Appointment Booking, Password Reset, Insurance FAQ, Contact (shared stylesheet)

Standard/Heuristic: WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value; WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard
Location: Appointment Booking page, Confirm Appointment button
Observation: Confirm button is a styled div with a click handler; no accessible name or role, and it can't be reached by keyboard.
Impact: Screen reader and keyboard users can't complete a booking at the final step.
Recommendation: Use a native button element with visible text "Confirm appointment".
At a Glance: Screen reader and keyboard users can't press the final button that confirms an appointment.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/book; `div.btn-confirm`; axe rule button-name / aria-command-name

Location: Body text, form helper text, and footer links on all audited pages
Observation: Body copy is #8A8A8A on #FFFFFF (3.5:1) and helper text is #A0A0A0 (2.6:1); both are below the 4.5:1 minimum for normal text.
Impact: Patients with low vision, older patients, and anyone reading on a phone outdoors will struggle to read core content.
Recommendation: Darken the body text token to at least #595959 (7:1) and helper text to at least #767676 (4.5:1).
At a Glance: Most of the site's text is too light to read comfortably for patients with low vision.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/, /book, /reset-password, /insurance-faq, /contact; axe rule color-contrast, 47 nodes across 5 pages

Standard/Heuristic: WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification; WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color
Location: Appointment Booking page, patient details form
Observation: Invalid fields are marked only with a red border; no error text is shown and nothing is announced to screen readers.
Impact: Colorblind and screen reader users can't tell which field is wrong or why, compounding UH-001.
Recommendation: Show a text error next to each invalid field, link it with aria-describedby, and summarize errors at the top of the form.
At a Glance: When the booking form has an error, only a red outline shows it, which many patients can't see or hear.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/book; submitted with empty date of birth; red border only; VoiceOver announced nothing

Observation: The reset form requires solving a drag-the-puzzle-piece CAPTCHA with no alternative method.
Impact: Patients with motor or cognitive disabilities may be locked out of their account.
Recommendation: Replace the puzzle with a non-interactive bot check (e.g. invisible challenge or rate limiting) or offer an email-link alternative.
At a Glance: Some patients with disabilities can't get past the password reset puzzle, so they can't get back into their account.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/reset-password; puzzle CAPTCHA required before submit; no audio or alternate option offered

Observation: Question headings jump from H1 to H4, and answers are in non-semantic divs, so the page has no usable heading outline.
Impact: Screen reader users can't skim the questions by heading and must listen to the whole page.
Recommendation: Use H2 for each FAQ category and H3 for each question.
At a Glance: Screen reader users can't jump between questions on the insurance FAQ page.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/insurance-faq; axe rule heading-order; heading outline: h1 > h4 x 38

Location: Primary buttons on all audited pages
Observation: Primary actions use three different button styles (filled teal, outlined navy, and text link with arrow) with no clear rule for which is used where.
Impact: The most important action on each page doesn't consistently stand out, so patients take longer to find it.
Recommendation: Define one primary, one secondary, and one tertiary button style and apply them consistently.
At a Glance: The main action on each page looks different from page to page, so it's harder to spot.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/ (hero), /book (Continue), /contact (Send); compared rendered styles

Observation: The hero image is 1200 px wide and is stretched to fill wide screens, so it looks blurry above about 1440 px.
Impact: Slightly lowers the polish of the first impression on large monitors.
Recommendation: Serve a 2400 px source via srcset.
At a Glance: The homepage photo looks blurry on large screens.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/; hero.jpg natural width 1200 px rendered at 1920 px

Standard/Heuristic: Navigation labeling; findability of top tasks
Observation: "Pay a Bill" and "Patient Portal" are only in the footer; the main navigation is organized around the organization ("About Us", "Our Services", "Resources") rather than patient tasks.
Impact: Two of the most common patient tasks are hard to find, which drives calls to the front desk.
Recommendation: Add "Pay a bill" and "Patient portal" to the header utility bar and test task-based labels for the main menu.
At a Glance: Patients can't find bill pay or the patient portal without scrolling to the footer.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/ header and footer nav; same on all audited pages

Observation: 38 questions are listed in one unbroken list with no categories, search, or in-page links.
Impact: Patients have to scan the whole page to find their question.
Recommendation: Group questions into 4-6 categories with jump links at the top.
At a Glance: The insurance FAQ is one long list, so answers are hard to find.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/insurance-faq

Standard/Heuristic: Health literacy: plain language (6th-8th grade target)
Observation: Answers read at about grade 13 and use unexplained terms such as "coordination of benefits", "out-of-network differential", and "prior authorization".
Impact: Many patients won't understand what they'll owe or what they need to do before a visit.
Recommendation: Rewrite answers at a 6th-8th grade level, define unavoidable terms in plain words, and lead with the answer.
At a Glance: The insurance answers are written for insurance experts, not patients.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/insurance-faq; Flesch-Kincaid grade 12.8 across all answers

Location: Appointment Booking page, step 3 submit button
Observation: The final button on the patient details step says "Submit".
Impact: Patients aren't sure whether pressing it books the appointment or just saves their details.
Recommendation: Label it "Book appointment".
At a Glance: The booking button says "Submit", which doesn't tell patients it books the appointment.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/book step 3

Observation: Entering an unrecognized email shows "Error 422: invalid input".
Impact: Patients don't know whether they mistyped their email or don't have an account.
Recommendation: Say what happened and what to do: "We couldn't find an account with that email. Check the spelling or create an account."
At a Glance: The password reset error is technical and doesn't tell patients what to do next.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/reset-password; submitted test@nonexistent.example

Observation: Patients must create an account (with email verification) before they can see any available appointment times; there is no guest option.
Impact: New patients, the group most likely to be booking, hit a sign-up wall before seeing whether a time works for them.
Recommendation: Show availability first and ask for account details only at confirmation; offer guest booking.
At a Glance: New patients have to create an account before they can even see open appointment times.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/book redirects to /register when not signed in

Observation: The reset link expires after 10 minutes; an expired link sends the patient to the homepage with no message.
Impact: Patients who don't check email right away end up back at the start with no idea what went wrong.
Recommendation: Extend the link to at least 60 minutes and show an "This link has expired - send a new one" page.
At a Glance: Password reset links expire quickly and fail silently, so patients get stuck.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/reset-password with test account; opened link after 12 minutes; redirected to /

Location: Appointment Booking page, date picker at 375 px
Observation: The week-view date picker is fixed at 640 px wide, so at phone width Thursday through Sunday are cut off and the page scrolls sideways.
Impact: Mobile patients can't see or choose late-week appointments without awkward side-scrolling.
Recommendation: Switch to a single-column day list or a swipeable week view below 640 px.
At a Glance: On phones, half the appointment calendar is cut off.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/book step 2; iPhone 13 emulation (390 px) and 375 px viewport

Observation: The phone number in the header is plain text, not a tel: link.
Impact: Mobile patients have to copy or memorize the number to call.
Recommendation: Wrap the number in a tel: link.
At a Glance: Patients on phones can't tap the phone number to call.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/ header; same on all pages

Location: Contact page and Appointment Booking page
Observation: Neither page says to call 911 for emergencies, and the contact form invites patients to "describe your symptoms" without stating a response time.
Impact: A patient with urgent symptoms could use the contact form and wait for a reply.
Recommendation: Add a prominent "If this is an emergency, call 911" notice and state the expected response time on contact and booking pages.
At a Glance: The site never tells patients to call 911 in an emergency, and the contact form asks for symptoms.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/contact, /book

Standard/Heuristic: Privacy and trust signals for health information
Observation: The form asks for date of birth and symptoms but has no notice about how health information is used or protected, and no link to the privacy policy.
Impact: Patients may hesitate to share needed information, or share it without understanding the risk.
Recommendation: Add a short privacy note above the submit button with a link to the privacy policy; consider removing symptom fields from an unsecured form.
At a Glance: The contact form asks for health details without saying how they're protected.
Evidence: https://example-site.com/contact
